title: Overview: the big ideas
summary: The chapter's key concepts and how its sections fit together.

blocks.md: Welcome to **Data Selection** (Vol I). This overview gives you the chapter's big ideas before the section-by-section lessons. Read the claims once, flip the flashcards, then take the warm-up quiz: it is fine to miss questions here, the lessons that follow fill the gaps.

Training pays to acquire, label, score, move, and process examples even though their learning value differs. Large datasets contain redundant, noisy, or target-misaligned samples, while scarce regions may lack the cases a model needs, such as the rare conditions under which a deployed system is most likely to fail.

rows: A training-time claim for data selection holds only if selection time plus subset training time is less than full training time at matched quality and coverage, so scorer size and refresh rate, not the retained fraction, decide whether selection is a net saving.

Sample value is learning per unit of training compute (the information-compute ratio), learning-curve metrics show whether a reduction held quality, and a gain in data value becomes a throughput gain only when the run is compute-bound and the saved work is on the critical path.

Controlled sweeps fit a compute-optimal balance of about 20 tokens per parameter, so a run whose unique tokens per parameter sit well below it is data-starved and repeats its corpus, which is the regime where selection rather than more compute moves the run toward the frontier.

Selection removes accelerator work but adds host hashing, scoring passes, scattered reads, and shard coordination, so a retained subset saves reads only if materialized into its own shards, and data echoing recovers idle accelerator cycles when host preparation is the slow stage.

Deduplication, quality pruning, and coreset selection shrink training work before training, but a score ranking must be constrained by per-class or per-slice coverage floors, which carry an explicit opportunity cost and can make a budget infeasible.

Because sample value changes as the model learns, curriculum learning reorders data by difficulty and pacing, and active learning turns labeling into a query loop whose label saving must be measured against a budget-matched random baseline after pool-scoring cost.

When the pool lacks the needed cases, augmentation and generative synthesis replace curation at a per-sample cost against realism, the domain gap needs randomization, adaptation, and a real-data anchor, and recursive training risks model collapse.

Semi-supervised and self-supervised learning trade extra training compute for fewer task labels, valid only when the unlabeled pool matches the target distribution, and a foundation model pays off only when pretraining is amortized across enough downstream tasks.

Total data cost is acquisition plus labeling plus storage plus processing, and a selection investment is judged by amortized return across all the runs it serves, so a pipeline that loses money on one run can pay across a campaign.
